Let Sleeping Dogs Lie

by Lilliae

Summary

He dredged through months slumbering and waking with a lover and a small checklist of tasks to greet him in the morning. Further back to months of restless nights and short naps through the day but nothing much to do. Then to a time of sleeping the days away in the closest thing he could get to fading entirely from existence.

In all that time, he couldn’t recall a single dream. It wasn’t merely the hazy content of a mind teetering between the sleeping and waking world that was beyond his grasp. There were no interrupted nights nor early morning. No racing heart nor stray thought of how strange that dream had been before the strangeness itself vanished back into the depths of his mind.

Nothing. His nights were empty.

…

Phainon must have been able to dream. Once. It was just another thing he had lost along the way, up an insurmountable journey, in wait for someone else to take his responsibilities to that final end beyond his reach.

For Amphoreans, sleep comes with the risk of reliving nightmares taken from the small eternity of their memories. The one exception is Phainon, who can no longer dream at all.

Notes

Let sleeping dogs lie - an English proverb suggesting to leave dormant controversies undisturbed even if they are unresolved.

See the end of the work for more notes

chapters.title: Let Sleeping Dogs Lie
chapters.html:
With the sky once again the plaything of the sun and moon, the nights of Amphoreus’ citizens were plagued with strange dreams. An excess of 33 million eternal recurrences fostered more memories than any ordinary mind should feasibly withstand. Yet, the new world didn’t collapse under the weight of the memories that had created it, and life strode into the long-awaited tomorrow. 

It took several months for the skulking truth to surface: the moment Amphoreus transcended from electrical signals into tangible lands and people, these memories were realised as facts and not experiences in the minds of their beholders. The events and its emotions were known but not felt. A distinction people only realised once that switch devastatingly flipped. 

Dissociation. Mental breakdowns. Catatonia. 

Patients entered the Twilight Courtyard in small numbers that slipped beneath notice in the chaos of rebuilding and fending off intergalactic establishments with too much interest in the newborn planet. It was a nonissue until Hyacine dropped a stack of parchment onto the table of Marmoreal Palace’s meeting room and declared a crisis of the mind. 

Everyone knew that the sun had been extinguished innumerable times over; devoured by an unrelenting corruption that pursued the reignited sun into the tomorrow that was really yesterday. They had observed it, dreaded it, scrambled to prevent it only to fail.

All of which was different from the panicterrorgrief that came to haunt their dreams. New and old information compounding upon themselves, the only time the mind was free to parse through that near eternal nightmare was within the depths of sleep. 

Under such strained time and resources, the Grove tentatively declared that there wasn’t a solution at present. The body worked in mysterious but self-regulating ways and these dreams comprised of relapsed memories would need to run their course. 

Manpower was a resource all of its own and stretched as thin as the rest. So it had taken the combined efforts of numerous Chrysos Heirs to corral Phainon into much too frequent checkups at the Courtyard. There were people in greater need of an assessment from a physician as talented as Hyacine, and any number of ways Phainon’s time could be better spent than at the Courtyard. 

But Anaxa had rapped his knuckles against Phainon’s forehead and reminded him that twice as many memories were chained inside Phainon’s mind than everyone else. Then added a second dry reminder that only one person on Amphoreus had the power to destroy the newly formed planet and its surrounding solar systems in a brief moment of dissociation. 

Certainly persuasive arguments, as expected from his professor who spoke circles around others and taught Phainon to do the same. But Mydei had claimed it wouldn’t do for his husband to be so stubborn and Phainon immediately agreed to every appointment necessary. 

The Courtyard was busy as usual but Phainon’s eye was drawn past the throngs of people to Little Ica floated ominously by the entrance. Its dark eyes seemed to find him before he was even in view and  latched on, leaving no possibility of escape. To think Hyacine had such little faith in him when he had been true to his word in the past months!

He was almost insulted the first time he was provided an escort. Now he simply revealed the pouch of chimera biscuits he had baked with Mydei the day prior, and offered it to Little Ica. It chirped happily, spinning in circles before bowing its head to let Phainon hook the drawstring around its neck. Satisfied with its haul, it led the way towards Hyacine’s office where they arrived just in time for her door to open and her previous patient to exit. 

Prominent bruises sagged beneath the man’s eyes and his pale, unsteady hands clutched a small amphora of medicine Phainon recognised because he had seen it prescribed many times over. Calming draughts. Hyacine probably tried to prescribe sleeping aids too but was refused. The possibility of being trapped in a previously lived nightmare was too daunting. 

It was exhausting work to be the supportive pillar of all sorrowing souls seeking a cure for their ailments, yet Hyacine smiled when she greeted him warmly, “Phainon, you made it. How have you been?”

Although he had hinted in the past that he was more than content for her to use his appointments to set aside the burden of that unwavering, calm benignity, she had declined to treat him too differently from her other patients. 

The most he could do was grin back with equal cheer. “I’m happy to report no issues at all.”

“Good to hear. Let’s start with the physical exam to be certain.”

While Little Ica retreated to its bed and munched on its biscuits in peace, Hyacine conducted a preliminary height and weight check. Then she poked and prodded in search of skin marred by fresh burn marks or cracking open along the fault lines of old scars. She examined his eyes and mouth for an inexplicable dryness. She checked his reflexes in case of damaged muscles or nerves. When those yielded ordinary results, she did a final read of his internal and external body temperature. 

“All done,” she declared, typing notes into her big teleslate as she backed into her seat. “You’re in perfect physical health.”

The results were as expected. So long as Mydei was in Okhema rather than handling affairs in Castrum Kremnos, Phainon was guaranteed to cook and eat healthily, get lots of exercise in as they competed over inane things or threw themselves into a friendly spar, and even sleep well with Mydei’s soothing presence at his side. 

He nodded, humming so she could hear him even with her head down typing up a few brief notes for later, but remained seated in wait for the next examination. 

“How have you been feeling lately?” Hyacine threw out the broad opening question that that rarely yielded noteworthy results.

He would have preferred any number of physical examinations before answering even the singular question. “Good?” The inflection wasn’t quite right and Hyacine peered up at him with the slightest signs of disapproval. He cleared his throat. “Good. I have more time on my hands than I’m used to.”

While his domestic life was fairly routine, his daily life was much less established as he flitted between whatever needed to be done and whichever one of his fellow Chrysos Heirs needed a hand. Yet there was never enough to fill his days. He knew they needed the extra help and they knew he had the time; however, he frequently found himself wandering Okhema without much to do. Even when he sought out extra tasks from friends or civilians, they would politely redirect him and insist they could handle it. 

Everyone wanted him to rest. He just didn’t know how to do nothing. 

“But I’m taking your advice from the last checkup,” he hastily added. “Lots of, ah, me time.”

He had dabbled in a few hobbies, picking up and putting down instruments, or chisel for a paintbrush, only to discover he wasn’t particularly talented with anything that wasn’t a sword or kitchen utensils. He had simply never dedicated the time to such pursuits in the past.

Often he ended up in the Garden of Life, sitting on the grass with a few chimeras for company and basking in the sunlight. Real sunlight and not the light of the Dawn Device, now extinguished in the distance without threat of a darkened sky caving in.

Hyacine nodded approvingly. “There’s no harm in taking time for yourself to unwind. Even if you think you’re being unproductive, the mind needs time to decompress. Speaking of, how have you been sleeping?”

“I wake up feeling refreshed.”

“Any memory relapse dreams?” 

“Nope,” he answered confidently. The same as he had in all preceding months. Only a few questions left and Phainon would be free to meet Mydei for lunch.

But Hyacine, mouth already open with a follow-up question, paused. That was a bad sign but then her lips thinned and that was an even worse one. “What about normal dreams?” It was not one of the usual questions that Phainon was prepared for and the confusion must have been evident because Hyacine elaborated, “Regular dreams. Unrelated to the cycles.“

He stared as she wrangled the frown off her face but her brows, despite lacking a visible crease, were so subtly pinched. She didn’t rescind her strange question. 

He tilted his head. Lost. “Like… walking out of a room and falling and waking up? Or suddenly being back in Anaxa’s classroom but it’s Castorice pointing a bubble gun at me because I forgot to hand in an assignment on time?”

Her perturbed features smoothed with a relieved exhale. “Yes. Those. So you’ve been having those.”

Ordinary dreams that could range from the mundane to the absurd to the scary. Anything so long as they weren’t a new experience of old memories. And yet…

“Not recently.”

The uneasiness returned. “What do you consider recently?”

He nibbled his inner cheek, forcing his mind to wind backwards. He dredged through months slumbering and waking with a lover and small checklist of tasks to greet him in the morning. Then further back to months of restless nights and short naps through the day but nothing much to do. Then to a time of sleeping the days away in the closest thing he could get to fading entirely from existence. 

In all that time, he couldn’t recall a single dream. It wasn’t merely the hazy content of a mind teetering between the sleeping and waking world that was beyond his grasp. There were no interrupted nights nor early morning. No racing heart nor stray thought of how strange that dream had been before the strangeness itself vanished back into the depths of his mind. Not even the openings of a brief conversation with any companions about an interesting dream. 

Nothing. His nights were empty. 

Behind his closed eyelids, he had to peer even further back in time to answer, “Before Irontomb was defeated.”

“Phainon,” she said and he hadn’t realised his mistake until he opened his eyes. Wide eyes, mouth agape and hands clutched around her teleslate—horrified. “That was almost a year ago.”

He hoped to reassure her with his chuckle but considered it may have been a lost cause. “Wow. Time really flies. If it were something serious then surely it would have made itself known before now.”

Her smile disagreed. It was the one reserved for difficult patients and Phainon wouldn’t deny he had been on the receiving end a few times when he deemed an injury too minor for a visit to the Courtyard. Of course, he ended up in front of Hyacine all the same and she reminded him about the importance of maintaining his health. The warmth behind her smile was oddly jarring against the underlying authority.

This was her domain after all, as much as the sky itself, and her level tone implied consequences to be incurred by disobedience, as she commanded, “Call Mydei and inform him that you’re being transported to the Grove for a more thorough checkup.” Before he could ask for more details, she scrolled through her teleslate and raised it to her ear. “Professor Anaxa, we’ve come across a situation.”

Phainon’s brows rose but Hyacine was too busy working her large teleslate while she spoke with Anaxa to notice. This was not how this appointment was supposed to go but it felt too late to change course. He could only be helplessly swept along the current. 

“Yes, that’s right,” she said after a brief pause that must have been Anaxa on the other side. Another pause. “We’re on our way.” She pocketed her teleslate, looking at Phainon once again. “Shall I call Mydei for you?” 

A call from Hyacine and the whole city would be on high alert when Mydei was spotted rushing at full speed to the Twilight Courtyard.

“I can handle it,” he assured her, for the good of everyone. She squinted but nodded and excused herself to inform her imminent absence to her colleagues. He really didn’t understand the urgency but waited for Mydei to answer his teleslate. “Hello, my dear husband.”

“Hello. What happened?”

He pouted, knowing Mydei couldn’t see him but ensuring it was audible enough for him to imagine. “Why do you assume something happened? Maybe I just thought you missed the sound of my voice.”

“I’ve heard it. And I’ll hear it again when I see you tonight.” 

“Wait wait,” Phainon surrendered their little game quicker than usual. Before Mydei really did hang up and Hyacine returned to take matters into her own hands. 

Static buzzed in his ear; the call was ongoing but Mydei stayed silent on the other end. Phainon mentally cursed himself. He had wanted to spare Mydei any and all distress within his power, but he could practically hear Mydei’s mind catching hold of loose threads and untangling possibilities. 

“What happened?” he repeated, sterner without the quiet playfulness softening the edge. 

“I’m not sure,” he admitted lamely because all Mydei’s attention had concentrated on his voice and would detect a lie, which would only worry him more. “Hyacine wants me to visit the Grove. Today.”

“Anaxagoras?”

“Naturally.”

Mydei hummed, short and low. “All right.” 

Then didn’t say any more. 

“All right then,” Phainon echoed dumbly. 

Mydei huffed a laugh. “What would you like me to say? Stay safe? Do as you’re told?” 

“Whatever you say, my dear husband,” he crooned, sickeningly sweet yet beneath it was the sincerity that he meant every word. 

It earned a little chuckle, so soft it was almost inaudible across the distance and static. “Go, and come home hale and whole.” 

He couldn’t contain his smile and wouldn’t want to. He only wished Mydei was here to see it for himself, and allow Phainon to witness him equally lovestruck. “I will.” 

A growing network of Century Gates sprawled outwards with Okhema at its heart. They ordinarily functioned on a strict schedule—specific days assigned to specific places, or organised around a particularly large caravan of people and goods brought to Aglaea’s attention with a humble request—but a simple message from Hyacine to Tribbie opened a discrete Century Gate opened between the Courtyard and Anaxa’s office.

Leaned against his desk, Anaxa was poised for their arrival. His only greeting was a simple gesture, ordering Phainon to sit as though the he were still a student and the clock had struck the beginning of their lesson.

He began without preamble, “I familiarised myself with Hyacine’s notes. Describe your dreams from the eternal recurrences. Any and all that you remember. No matter how insignificant it seems.”

In all honesty he would rather not. However, sat before the two of them, Hyacine’s hands clasped in front of her as she smiled with encouragement unable to waver and Anaxa’s arms crossed with his eye narrowed close to a glare that denoted concentration more than anger, and there was no other option.

They were concerned about Phainon. Because of Phainon. He had promised to be a model patient and he strived to be true to his word. Despite how his toes curled with the urge to flee, he lowered his eye to the desk’s smooth stone and cast his mind back. 

Bleeding feet, burning body, a stone boulder up a steep incline that would roll back down as soon as he approached the precipice. 

Hazy eyes, smoke and iron on his tongue, flames within his chest fuelled by an overwhelming hatred. 

Glaring red lights, twisting metal vines, a scorching blade in one hand that extinguished in a single hit and tumbled down down down and took him with it. 

There were so many more than he first recalled. The weathered top of a single broken column, peeking through the thin earthen cover, was only one of many hidden artefacts of the past, indicative of the rest clustered together just waiting to be uncovered. The more he dug the more he found. 

Faint images of golden blood, of empty eyes, of a starry sky illuminated by thirteen constellations. The distant sound of breaths rattling off a mask and hollowed body, of voices he couldn’t hear beneath an inferno raging in his ears but he could feel off fragile skin, of a machine mocking him with words that blurred into static. 

When everything was said and done, stood centre stage upon the archeological site of his subconscious mind, fully excavated and exposed for all to see, he realised the only thing surrounding him on every side was himself.

His past memories bleeding into his present in a prelude to his future. 

A glimpse of Anaxa’s pinched brows, hand cupped to his chin, as he gazed at Phainon like he could pierce him through to the soul and dissect it in pursuit of knowledge, and Phainon knew that he had realised it too.

Phainon must have been able to dream. Once. It was just another thing he had lost along the way, up an insurmountable journey, in wait for someone else to take his responsibilities to that final end beyond his reach. 

In a rustle of parchment, Anaxa unfurled a blank scroll across his desk and grabbed a reed pen. Despite the convenience of a teleslate, he had always preferred ink and parchment or chalk on a chalkboard, and he began to etch lines with the same fervour as alchemical equations. 

He etched a small circle and a horizontal line that branched into two. “Two of you existed in any given recurrence, yet you were still a single extrapolation from the same base code. Such an unforeseen variable must have strained the system, creating small processing errors where your two existences interacted, even on a subconscious level. Until—“ The branches ran parallel and then collapsed into one, “—it merged and re-stabilised.”

Hyacine traced the air above stark, damning lines. “Only to divide again shortly after.”

Anaxa cut off the cycle with a vertical line, continuing it on the other side in a new extrapolation before returning to the first and branching it to bypass the supposed finish line. The lined continued in parallel: two Phainon’s. Different yet inextricably intertwined at the source.

“I hadn’t considered it this way,” Anaxa admitted with a self-effacing frown. “I assumed the you carrying the Coreflames had emancipated yourself somehow and become rogue electrical signals or something of the sort. But for you to dream about past recurrences, both instances of you had to be connected so strongly that your separate consciousnesses could interweave when your sense of self was weakest.”

In his sleep. 

“Yes, isn’t that just fascinating,” Phainon readily agreed. “Your mind is as sharp as always, Professor Anaxa. Mystery solved.”

“A year without a relapse dream,” Anaxa pressed onwards, so engrossed he didn’t so much as look up from the parchment. Phainon resigned himself to the true topic’s return. “It allowed your mind to do throughout what all of ours are being forced to do now: process your memories. We already tested your recall—it’s perfect. Beyond what an ordinary mind should recall in fact and emotion.”

Hyacine whispered like a eulogy and not a prayer, “Kephale never forgets.” 

While others could only relive the past though their dreams and nightmares, Phainon need only think and remember every sensation, even emotion, every terrible act by his own hand. They were all stored with perfect clarity, as if even the very first cycle were only a moment ago. 

As a blasphemer, disbelieving laughter an undercurrent his voice, Anaxa said, “Congratulations, you’ve found a way to excel once again.”

It was a sincere compliment for one of his own students, yet it sounded so sarcastic Phainon couldn’t help a small, self-deprecating chuckle. “Thank you, professor.”

“But that doesn’t explain why he isn’t experiencing normal dreams,” Hyacine pointed out.

Anaxa rapped his pen against the parchment. “The simplest solution is that his mind was so severely overworked for an extended period of time that it requires complete rest. Sleep is the time the mind processes and stores the day’s information. Since you haven’t noted any long-term memory issues, that part is still functioning but without the resources to spare to conjure up narratives, emotions and visual memories.“

Which meant, excluding a single function, Phainon’s brain operated fine.

“So,” Phainon ventured tentatively, “from the sounds of it, there are no issues.”

Anaxa glanced at Hyacine, as a physician and colleague, and back to Phainon as their patient. “I suppose not.”

“We should consider doing a sleep study. To be certain,” Hyacine suggested in polite disagreement. 

At the mention of an experiment, Anaxa’s lip pulled into an exhilarated grin and Phainon no longer feared for his soul but his body was another matter. “It would be of interest to see which parts of your brain are in use. That can be arranged.“

Both Hyacine and Anaxa agreed to oversee the experiment and that it was of utmost importance to begin outlining the research proposal immediately. The faster it was submitted, the faster they could begin, and the faster they could receive results that may bring about a solution. Although Phainon stayed, he had little input to give them when the entire thing was about him. 

Anaxa had conducted multiple experiments on him by now, predominantly aimed at understanding and mitigating the damages done to his body and psyche over the cycles but, despite being qualified, Phainon had little interest in designing the studies. His suggestions were usually limited to vetoing something he was uncomfortable with and Anaxa would nod before striking it from the proposal and moving on. Otherwise, he simply followed Anaxa’s intellectual curiosity and instincts that had brought him so far. 

The discussion dragged long as Anaxa began considering different draughts and decoctions that could impact the results, and Hyacine rejected or tentatively agreed based on their safety. Phainon doubted anything Anaxa fed him would do much damage—he had standards and Phainon had a particularly resilient body—but he appreciated her efforts. 

Thankfully, a knock on the office door interrupted them and opened before Anaxa could grant them entry. Phainon’s brows rose at the boldness, or foolishness, to brave a fresh bullet mark to the forehead. 

Except Phainon perked up, grinning, as Mydei softly closed the door behind him; quiet, as to not disrupt their discussion when all eyes had turned to him immediately. Even when Mydei moved with the lithe grace of a diligent hunter, somehow avoiding any incongruence with his bulkier physique, his sheer presence was simply too much to ignore. It demanded attention like storm clouds thundering over the horizon, smoke and fire flickering across the plains, the purest of gold amidst bronze.

Anaxa set his gun back down and tersely greeted, “Mydei.”

It was a far cry from Hyacine’s smile, more friend than physician, and the wiggle of her fingers in a wave. “Good evening, Mydei.”

“Anaxa. Hyacine,” he greeted with a nod to each in turn as he crossed the room to stand behind Phainon’s seat. 

Phainon tipped his head back, suppressing every instinct to smile at the casual hand Mydei laid over the back of his chair. Instead, he pouted. “Come for a checkup of your own? Something important seems to have slipped your mind.”

In retribution, Mydei pinched his nose and Phainon playfully tried to shake him off without much success. Mydei’s eyes crinkled and he let go, swooping down to peck the reddened tip of his nose. “Phainon.”

The appearance of a foul mood dissipated at once, replaced with him preening and nuzzling his cheek against Mydei’s forearm. “Mydei.”

“Is he free to go?” Mydei asked the other two, who were pointedly ignoring the affectionate displays that had become common sight. 

Hyacine’s nose scrunched as she considered. “It’s nothing so serious he needs to stay.”

With approval from the physician, Anaxa flapped his hand dismissively. “The proposal needs to be finalised and authorised. I’ll send you the details then.”

“Great!” Phainon hopped from his seat at the favourable verdict. “Thank you for your time, Hyacine, Anaxa.”

Mydei didn’t resist when Phainon slung an arm around his shoulder. “Thank you for the hard work.”

Hyacine’s grin brightened with a small chuckle, shaking her head. “No need to thank us. Remember, your next appointment is in three weeks.”

“See you then.”

They exchanged brief farewells and they had yet to reach the room’s threshold before Hyacine and Anaxa resumed their conversation. It was difficult to discern how much Mydei heard, much less understood, from the brief mentions of sleep and dreams when his head was down at his teleslate, allowing Phainon to guide him through the Grove’s winding hallways. Reconstruction efforts were considerably slower in the Grove than elsewhere, as the gouged and corroded wood was slowly recultivated rather than replaced with stone, so it could one day appear as it had once been. 

Phainon peered over Mydei’s shoulder as he messaged Tribbie, apologising for a second Century Gate request in such quick succession but she replied with a reassurance and cute sticker before the Gate opened for them to step through. 

His benign condition had caused so much more inconvenience than it was worth. His stomach churned from more than motionless sickness but they reappeared outside of Kephale Plaza and Mydei turned to him. His eyes, sharp and knowing yet devoid of judgment, jostled him from the downward spiral of his thoughts.

An apology, prepared to be playful yet genuine beneath it, stayed on his tongue. Mydei wasn’t one to be feebly forced into anything. He had followed Phainon to the Grove because he wanted to and to suggest otherwise with an apology, as though Phainon had foisted the task upon him, would be tantamount to dismissing Mydei’s actions. The care. The sincerity. 

So Phainon looped an arm over Mydei’s shoulder, fingers slipping between the metal chains and plates of his necklace warmed by his body heat, as he nuzzled his nose against Mydei’s temple. “Thank you for coming to get me.”

He kissed his cheek and Mydei hummed, steady and solemn despite leaning into every point of contact like a grumpily affectionate cat. “Did you forget? You lost. It’s your turn to cook tonight.”

At the reminder of his, albeit close, defeat in knucklebones the night before, his laugh broke across the swell of Mydei’s cheek. “You got me. I was planning to run away from my debts.”

“To think that Hyacine and Anaxa conspired with you.”

“I guess that means I’m their favourite patient. Well, Hyacine’s favourite patient. And Anaxa’s favourite test subject.”

Mydei didn’t fall for the bait—both, at some point or another, frequent patients and research subjects—and glanced at him sidelong, flat and unimpressed in contrast to the upturned corner to his lip. “Once they figure out how that mind of yours works, I’ll be sure to get them to tell me.”

He unleashed an offended, wounded noise but Mydei slipped a hand around his waist, ensuring Phainon followed as he began to walk them in the direction of home, and Phainon was pacified by a single squeeze. On many other occasions, he would keep up the act, cajoling concessions from Mydei while he played along by keeping them away only to acquiesce in the end. 

But Mydei had yet to ask how and why Phainon’s routine checkup had ended with him at the Grove of Epiphany and a new branch of research coming to fruition. Hyacine and Anaxa would have given him a thorough update if asked; however, his only concern had been whether Phainon was well enough to return home. Even as they closed off the rest of the world from the privacy of their home, he didn’t inquire further. Instead, he waited for Phainon to speak on his own terms. 

It was always like this: Mydei waiting for Phainon. Sometimes, he idly wondered if Mydei would ever grow bored of waiting for him. Yet even he couldn’t be so wilfully blind to ignore Mydei lurking, the most patient hunter, in justice of his epithet, like he could be satisfied watching Phainon come ever closer to being devoured, so wholly there was nothing left to hide, for another small eternity. 

Mydei knew the best of him, the worst of him, and the muddled mess in the middle. Still, he chose to lean against the counter with a chalice of pomegranate juice while Phainon prepared dinner for two in a home they shared. There had never been anywhere easier for Phainon to expose his weaknesses, his flaws, and he recounted his visit to clinic appointment that resulted in a new hypothesis. 

Without much to say while Phainon regaled the day’s events, Mydei finished his meal first and silently sat across the dining table. He watched Phainon eat, arms crossed and expression neutral, masking the thoughts visible in the brief moment they flitted across his eyes like sparks jumping to burn anew on fresh kindling elsewhere. 

Only once they were both finished did Mydei ask, “Do you miss dreaming?” 

Phainon’s laugh was more sardonic than he intended, burning his throat and teeth, but… “I didn’t realise there was anything to miss.”

It was much easier to notice the presence of something amiss than the absence of something entirely.

The acrimony never deterred Mydei and he leaned forward to set his arms on the table, closing the distance like he could reach across and snag onto the cloud of Phainon’s thoughts before they scattered. “Now you do. So do you miss it?”

It was generous to call those things across more than 33 million cycles dreams: the memories of his past self bleeding into his present self as they simultaneously roamed a world constructed by a system only meant to contain one and not both. The one and only time he had something that could be considered a real dream was when his mind was still whole in the very first cycle. 

No matter how much time passed, the Worldbearer never forgets. He could recall the outside world dreamed by a boy, of a peaceful village and its violent end haunting an adolescent, of deliverance and its mounting costs by a young man. But they accounted for the smallest slip of time. How could he feel the loss of something so inconsequential he barely had it at all?

“No.”

It was late and Mydei nodded, sitting back in his chair only to rise not long after and take their dishware to wash up while Phianon followed to keep him company. They left the topic behind on the dining table. The discussion moved on to a recipe the Trailblazer had sent Mydei from whatever new planet their journey among the stars had taken them to. 

With intergalactic trade agreements in place but yet to begin, it would be much too difficult to source all the exact ingredients. So Mydei had, rather painstakingly, extracted the flavour profile from the Trailblazer until Dan Heng took mercy upon him and inserted himself to answer all his questions in full. He hoped to attempt a recreation with things native to Amphoreus and, naturally, Phainon’s own expertise in the kitchen would be at his disposal. 

It would be a full day of brainstorming, experimenting, taste testing and passing the trial dishes amongst their friends to get a sense of which ones were the best. Phainon was looking forward to it. 

Rather than trek to Marmoreal Palace and back, they bathed at home and swiftly prepared for bed. Although Phainon knew he could only close his eyes and plunge into a darkness devoid of dreams, with Mydei’s head propped on the pillow beside him, expression easing with his breathing, his heart didn’t have the opportunity to be restless before it was soothed. Not serene enough to slumber, but he blinked drowsy eyes and felt content to lie in wait for sleep to find him.

Meanwhile, Mydei slept like the dead. To see someone who lived so loudly—titillating presence that charged the air like the moments before lightning struck, and a subdued voice that roared like thunder: rallying his people to arms or laying them to rest entirely—reduced to a deathly quiet stillness was frightening. Whether he watched Mydei fall asleep after a fatal injury that forced his soul to claw back into his body or he simply stumbled across him napping on the rooftops, Phainon had made the mistake of shaking him awake before he could think to check for a pulse numerous times in the past.

He never asked where he adopted such sleeping habits and Mydei never volunteered an explanation for why he preferred his back against a wall, body huddled into itself, like a child afraid to sprawl into more space than they were allowed. To be large. Noticeable. Vulnerable. 

There was no need for him to ask because, in some intangible way more emotion than fact, he already knew. The same way he knew, always, that it meant something when Mydei rolled onto his side to sleep with Phainon at his back. 

Although they fell asleep in each other’s arms, on the rare occasion Phainon woke in the night without disturbing Mydei from rest, he found they naturally drifted apart. Tonight was no different. Phainon must have fallen asleep because one moment they were side-by-side and the next Mydei had rolled to the other end of the kline. Since Mydei was a light sleeper, it took slow and consistent efforts to creep closer without waking him.

Mydei’s back was so still that the slightest movement forced Phainon to pause and wait for him to sink back into slumber. He was close enough for his hand to feel where Mydei’s body had warmed the mattress but the final stretch was the most tenuous. It demanded patience. 

Mydei’s back tensed. Then relaxed again and Phainon took a shallow breath, holding it as he prepared to close the last of the distance. Only for him to freeze as the sculpted muscles from his shoulders down to his scapulas twitched. Spasmed. The rest of him was motionless but the tension frantically tore through his hunched back and set his tattoos alight that illuminated the entire room in the pulsating red of a frenetic heartbeat. 

The colour protruded through his skin, body trembling as his blood crystallised and pierced through to the surface in the same pain he stoically endured. In sleep, he lacked the presence of mind to mask the agony and an anguished noise choked through the tremors.

Phainon reached to smooth a hand across his tense shoulders, his back, and coax him from whatever terrors had gripped him so tight his body needed to forge weapons and armour. Before his palm could flatten against the one spot in need of the most protection and yet frightfully bare, a weight slammed into his shoulder. He tipped onto his back with a grunt and the weight followed him down to trap him beneath unyielding muscle and crystal. 

Sat astride his stomach and blood hardened to a dagger to level at his throat, Mydei had him pinned. Far from the play fights of their spars, puppies snapping and mouthing at each other but letting go before they could truly maim, Mydei snarled like he couldn’t decide between slitting his throat or tearing it apart with bare teeth already gleaming red in the light of his tattoos.

Beneath Mydei’s hand crushing his ribs, his lungs strained for air but he didn’t breathe, neck stinging where the jagged crystal threatened to draw blood. He had spent millions of years choking on the scorching heat of the suns he swallowed again and again, heedless of how they charred his body to cinders. The thrashing instinct to survive that all living beings shared, even Mydei as he danced with the Hand of Shadow, embracing it only to slip free like the most elusive lover, had been burned out of Phainon. 

So he held still and waited for the frenzy to pass. For Mydei to realise he wasn’t a threat. The drowsiness had partially cleared but Mydei glared with wild eyes. What was he seeing? What memory had relapsed into his dreams? The faceless mask of a stranger covered in smoke and ash, or had it already shattered to reveal the near unrecognisable face entombed below?

Then Mydei blinked and the feral instinct of a cornered animal withdrew, skulking away into his subconscious, his memories, his dreams, and taking the suffocating pressure against Phainon’s lungs with it. He sucked in a sharp inhale but didn’t give it time to settle before he leveraged himself upright. 

There was too much space between them. Mydei so rarely retreated from battles of steel nor wits but, within the disrupted peace of their home, he had backed away onto his knees. His palms dug into his eyes and fingers clawed through his loose hair, tension hardening his body but not enough to fend off the tremors as his blood settled sluggish back into his veins and his skin molted its crystals without honing more—more armour, more weapons—letting them crumble to dust like the rest of him would follow in the next shuddering breath.

Phainon thumbed at his neck, checking for blood that could bring remorse but his finger came away clean. No blood, no crystals, and Mydei curled so small into himself with eyes shrouded in darkness. It was almost as though nothing had happened. 

Yet they were suspended in this terrible moment that refused to end, suffocating without hands nor blade.

Phainon’s hands trembled, scorned once, but he forced them to steady and shuffled on his knees with open arms, exposing a heart struck through and prepared for the well-deserved second blow, as he coaxed, “Hey. Come here.”

A deep breath heaved Mydei’s hunched shoulders and his palms pressed deep into his eyes a final time before they fell away. Reddened and bruised; heavy with an exhaustion more potent than the one that had put him to sleep. He searched Phainon’s expression, for fear, for hesitation, for appeasement, and down to his neck for even the thinnest slice of blood. 

Finding nothing, he tumbled into Phainon’s awaiting arms. He smoothed a hand through Mydei’s mussed hair, damp with a cold sweat, and the other looped around the arch of his spine. Slowly, he lowered them to their sides, tucking Mydei beneath his chin and entangling their legs but not too tight Mydei felt trapped. 

He knew. He already knew. Yet he couldn’t help but twist the dagger forged from the golden blood he had personally spilled and watched stain his hands. “What did you dream about?” 

“Drowning,” Mydei said, at once firm, unshaken, yet quieter than usual and that alone spoke volumes. “In my own blood.”

Phainon kissed the crown of his head. “And?”

“What else is there?” Mydei breathed a laugh so caustic it burned where it spilled from Mydei’s throat across Phainon’s clavicle, splattering like acid corroding through skin and bone down to his heart. “Who else has held the honour of killing me in any way that matters.”

After such an ordeal, he didn’t want to start an argument. He just wanted Mydei to be able to rest peacefully as he deserved. So he locked the apolity behind his teeth and tightened his arms around him in unspoken remorse that Mydei heard, felt, and responded to with a nudge of his forehead against Phainon’s clavicle. He held Mydei close as though he wouldn’t allow even death to separate them. Never mind that it had been Phainon’s own blade to part them. 

Now his hands, calloused and scarred but empty of a sword, brushed Mydei’s hair from his forehead to leave a kiss in its place before he began to speak about all sorts of inconsequential things. His voice rumbled from his chest into Mydei’s own, louder than the memory of choking on his own blood and falling to join the ruined battlefield darkened by the shadow of a thing more monster than man. 

When Mydei was lulled back to sleep and inevitably squirmed away, rolling into his own space where he could tuck himself tight like a child battered by sea and strife, Phainon let his hand lie slack in the distance between them. He closed his eyes and didn’t dream.

This wasn’t the first time a Chrysos Heir’s memories had relapsed in their dreams. If they discussed it amongst themselves and offered support through the ordeal of hopeless struggle and endless deaths, then Phainon wasn’t privy to it. The face of their tormentor didn’t offer much comfort. 

He could reasonably guess when one had occurred. Abruptly cancelled plans with a guilty promise to reschedule, a change in routine so they wouldn’t cross paths as usual, tasks reassigned seemingly at random. 

There were times when he had no need to guess. He knew it by Castorice’s wide-eyed flinch when Phainon initiated their newly familiar greeting of a hearty hug. By Cipher sliding a half-step in front of Aglaea when her ears twitched upon his arrival. By Anaxa fiddling with his gun more than usual while explaining his findings. 

By Mydei awakening in the night with intent to kill. 

He knew and he always smiled before leaving them the space and time to process their anguish, their grief, their suffering at his hands. They were scars he had carved into their souls and, ripped open mercilessly in the night, the fresh wounds needed to heal in peace. Once the pain had dulled into a hardly noticeable ache, their relationships shook off the reticence and fell back into their usual rhythm. 

So Phainon, feeling as though he hadn’t rested at all, rose before first light. Since Mydei’s rest had been disrupted in the night, he was entrenched in deeper sleep than normal and didn’t stir when Phainon slid from the kline. He snuck around the house like a common thief as he washed off the remnants of poor sleep, dressed himself in a simple chiton, and left empty handed. 

Without plans, he wandered through the waking city. The vendors were setting up their stalls in the marketplace and he offered a hand here and there, making conversation until the smell of breakfast wafted through the air. He purchased some golden honeycakes and fruit but took them to eat elsewhere; he didn’t want to worry the vendors that their food was amiss when they saw his voracious appetite shrunken to near nothing. 

He ended up on Dawncloud where no council meetings for the day meant only those seeking out a sunrise view or Okhema’s library crossed his path. People who knew him as everyone else did: the unbreaking Deliverer and nothing less but nothing more either. No one questioned him as he approached Kephale, reduced to a statue, a landmark, with no purpose.

The Worldbearing altar was empty but he bypassed the steps and circled the platform to the very back where he sat hidden from the view of all except the remains of a long departed god. There was no reason for Mydei to come here and he took his first real breath of the morning as he leaned against the wall, dangled his legs over the edge, and opened his box of honeycakes. 

Of all the Chrysos Heirs, the only one to never hear the voice of their fore-bearer was him. Whether he was born before or after Kephale departed from Amphoreus, leaving their legacy in the false sun upon their shoulders waiting for the dawn to arrive, the results were always the same. Kephale, the Titan of Worldbearing, the Chrysos Heir to previously claim the Worldbearing Coreflame, the one to remake the world they had known into the Amphoreus that had welcomed the next set of actors reenacting the same play, never spoke to Phainon. 

Even as their voice was heard by priests and supplicants, in the face of the next Worldbearer Kephale fell silent. It had been the source of Phainon’s grievances numerous times, subjecting him to the questioning of the council doubting his legitimacy to inherit the Coreflame of a god that refused to acknowledge him. Phainon hadn’t understood then but—when those recurrences came to their inevitable end and he was faced with his self that had been denied the dawn, and two collapsed into one being—he realised that there was simply nothing that could be said to the one destined to shoulder such a burden. 

Kephale was long gone, as was the lonely Khaslana that, in a moment of lucidity, had beseeched the silent god to answer him: what choice would the previous Deliverer have made? What solution would they have found that he had failed to grasp? He never received an answer before he was called to take the next bloodstained step on his journey. 

So perhaps it was strange that he felt a kinship with the one who shared the title of Worldbearer. They walked different paths but the task was the same: bear the blazing sun until the pale dawn breaks.

For once, he didn’t mind the silence upon the Worldbearing altar as he snacked on his foods from the marketplace, idly scrolled his teleslate, and tipped his head back to watch the sky change from dawn to dusk coloured by soft hues and gentle light. He could have slept under the stars and Kephale’s watch but his teleslate vibrated with a message. A simple thing from Aglaea: you have a room in Marmoreal Palace.

Her golden web was cast over Amphoreus, primarily to facilitate communication while new technology was in the process of being implemented. Although her vision had been restored, the threads continued to reveal sights beyond her eyes and it seemed she didn’t approve of his vagrancy. 

It had been a long time since he used the room within Marmoreal Palace reserved just for him. Aglaea kept it thoroughly clean in case he wanted to stay when work ran long; however, he politely declined every time. Nothing could rival the comforts of home. 

But, tonight, he wanted to respect Mydei’s space.

More often than not, it was his first residence upon his arrival in Okhema. It was sparsely decorated; a guest room without indication it belonged to anyone in particular. But it had been dusted recently and the kline freshly prepared along with a set of clean garments left folded on top. While he changed, he made a mental note to peruse the marketplace for something to Aglaea’s tastes. 

Then he sprawled on the blankets and cushions with a quiet sigh. They were perfumed with rose oil rather than pomegranates warmed by an underlying masculine scent, and mingled with wheat that Phainon could never detect but Mydei insisted was present. 

It wasn’t home but it was comfortable and he had hardly slept the night before. A little shuffling on his back and he sank into the mattress just right, eyes closing to languish in the passage of time bringing a new dawn—as many tomorrows as he needed to wait. 

He had yet to doze off before the door opened but he didn’t open his eyes. It was likely a Garmentmaker sent by Aglaea with food. His stomach was twisted too tight to eat much but the last thing he wanted was to reject her hospitality or worry her enough to come pity him in person. 

A quiet noise suspended his thoughts. It was something grazing the tile floor. A footstep when Garmentmaker’s drifted. 

He opened his eyes and tried to sit up but the intruder had swiftly crossed the room and a solid weight shoved him back down. Supple skin, contoured muscle, pomegranates and other bath oils—known to him even in sleep. 

Mydei sprawled across his lap, chin propped on Phainon’s stomach where his hair, damp from the baths, dripped water in translucent splotches along his white chiton. His expression was set stern yet not quite steady in his usual stoicism. Something was hidden in his face, searching Phainon’s own, but it was utterly indiscernible to Phainon’s scrambling mind. 

Phainon tried to shuffle upright but Mydei’s arms around his waist lacked even that slight give, and he chuckled nervously. “Hello, Mydei. What brings you here?”

“Did we move?”

Phainon’s mouth opened. Shapeless air passed through. “Excuse me?”

“Did we move house?”

“No?”

“Yet you intended to sleep here,” Mydei stated. Knowing, yet steadfast rather than indignant. Not a challenge nor an accusation.  

“I…” The usual lie or outrageous comment sat poised on his tongue, as though this were normal. As though Phainon had the right to be anything other than accommodating and penitent. “I wanted to give you some space. To process.”

Finally, Mydei’s stone face, restraint in every muscle, gave way to a sour twist of his lips and narrowed eyes. Unimpressed. “Remind me when I requested space.”

The silence spoke for him. 

By all accounts, it was Mydei’s victory but he didn’t appear satisfied when he squeezed Phainon in his arms and turned his cheek into Phainon’s stomach. “It aches.”

At the admittance of pain from Mydei of all people, Phainon lurched and reached for his discarded teleslate—he needed to call Hyacine immediately. This was an emergency—but whatever weight Mydei had been supporting on his own suddenly slumped across Phainon’s torso. Unless he wanted to tussle with Mydei on the kline, wholeheartedly attempting to throw him to the ground and undoubtedly earn Aglaea’s ire in the process, he was pinned where Mydei wanted him. 

In this position, he could only pause, uncertain but unable to search Mydei’s features and discern the rules to this latest bout. Mydei had only given him one hint. 

“What aches?” Phainon murmured.

There was something heavy in the air, thick with potential in the same way dried kindling was perfect for a spark. Volatile, with a result that could be beautiful or disastrous. 

“Where else?” he grumbled. 

His eyes fell upon the exposed hump of Mydei’s back, tracing the vivacious red of his tattoos down to a bare bit of skin and through to the notch of his spine underneath. 

His throat clogged with emotion swelling up from his chest, heart as twitchy as his hands curled into the sheets. He swallowed it down. “What can I do to help?”

“Just…” His sigh sank beneath Phainon’s chiton, tingling across the planes of his stomach. He shifted and his hair parted around his reddened ears. “Use your hands.”

The colour was darkest at the very tips, red stark against Mydei’s light hair. He was embarrassed and, knowing that, brought the same heat to Phainon’s face. All his other worries seemed so inconsequential and, tentatively, he cupped his hands over that old and brittle weakness. 

“I’m not wounded,” Mydei chided at the featherlight touch, fearing the bone would crumble to dust. To ash on the wind. “It’s merely phantom pain.” 

From having his tenth thoracic vertebrae shattered again and again. 

“Have you had them before?”

It was straightforward question with one of two answers but Mydei remained silent like there was more to it that must be considered.

“Yes,” he relented the truth. 

Yet he hadn’t mentioned it before now, and they both knew why. That guilt, that self-loathing, festering in Phainon’s heart weakened by the scorching suns blazing within it. He was learning, slowly, to cut the rot out before it could spread but it had to be done with steady hands and a clear mind. 

For now, his heads were steadfast as he pressed his fingers on either side of Mydei’s spine. His shoulders hitched with a sharp, quiet breath and Phainon paused. It had sounded like surprise more than pain but he waited for confirmation.

Then Mydei relaxed against him and Phainon pressed a little harder, watching the tension melt from Mydei’s back and his next exhale felt like relief. Gently, Phainon massaged at the notch of Mydei’s spine and moved outwards into the surrounding muscle. 

“Tell me. Next time,” Phainon coaxed, rubbing his thumbs in smooth circles, alternating between muscle and bone beneath thin skin.

The gentle touches elicited small sighs and Mydei hummed. “All right.” 

Sprawled limp across Phainon’s lap, he was reminiscent of an overgrown house cat. A lion seemingly domesticated but capable of goring out Phainon’s heart with his claws or jugular with his teeth and Phainon could practically hear him purring. It was an honour to have him vulnerable beneath Phainon’s hands shaped by hatred and violence, but an honour Mydei had willingly bestowed upon him. 

Or perhaps Phainon had been the one tamed and taken home. Mydei had let him have his fun for the day without giving chase so they both could breathe easier. Once night fell it was time for Phainon to come home so they could shake off their troubles, sleep easy and wake up beside each other.

He dug into the muscles around Mydei’s scapulas, loosening out the knots with his thumbs. “Were you waiting for me? At home?” 

“Of course.” 

“It’s always you waiting for me,” Phainon murmured. 

And Phainon running away. A coward who fled and hid rather than confront the past, the truth, as it came to haunt him. 

Mydei squeezed him in a hug that Phainon habitually reciprocated. “You waited far longer. I’m just catching up. Don’t forget that.”

His eyes stung and he closed them, left grounded in the darkness by the comfortable weight over his torso. “All right then.”

He fell asleep with his hands over Mydei’s back and Mydei’s head propped over his heart pulsing with the sun’s radiance as much as blood. But it was slow, steady, and remained as such through the night as their bodies stayed together, melding into each other starting from where they were weakest. 

After a quick morning bath, they returned home and got started on that recipe from the Trailblazer. The plan had been postponed a day but neither of them were bothered by it as they manoeuvred around the kitchen; smooth and instep. 

While it was baking in the oven, Mydei wiped down the countertops and Phainon washed the dishes. They wouldn’t know the results for another few hours but Phainon was hopeful. 

“Last night,” Mydei said, eyes down on the countertop. From where Phainon was standing it was spotless, yet he dragged the cloth over it again. “I dreamed that I couldn’t find you. Not at home. Not anywhere. You were gone. I thought you weren’t coming back.” 

Phainon didn’t know what to say. If one of them relapsed into their memories, whether in a dream or reality, and harmed the other in a fit of madness, Phainon had always assumed it would be his own hands to do it, always breaking the things most precious. 

Knowing it may be impossible was such a short-lived relief when he hadn’t needed his hands, nor a million memories clawing him into the darkness where the dawn couldn’t reach, to harm Mydei in a way that mattered. 

“But then I found you. Shrunken down to fit in my palm. So I commissioned a necklace you could comfortably sit inside while I carried you with me wherever I went,” Mydei said, so nonchalant that Phainon just…

Laughed. 

“Mydei,” he wheezed between fits of giggles, “what are you talking about?”

He shrugged and leaned his hip against the counter, flicking the cloth into the sink for a rinse, but shared Phainon’s bemusement in his quirked lip. “It was a dream.”

He snorted. “It was ridiculous.”

Mydei hummed his agreement but tilted his head, bangs and braid swaying, hands still upon his crossed arms so all his attention was on Phainon when his smile softened. “The nonsensical, the miserable, the pleasant—we’ll share them. From now on, I’ll entrust all my dreams to you.”

Tempered by the fondness bright in Mydei’s creased eyes and swelling in his own chest, he smiled. “I’d like that.”

Mydei nodded and pushed off the counter, a few steps swiftly closing the distance, so he could tug Phainon by the chin into a kiss. It wasn’t fair that his hands were wet from the sink or he would have grabbed Mydei by the hips and hauled him in for more when he broke away after something short and sweet but not satiating. 

“There’s something else,” Mydei said and sauntered past Phainon, out the kitchen, with nothing but a pat to his shoulder as consolation.

The few remaining bowls were scrubbed clean at speed and Phainon dried off his hands just as Mydei returned to the kitchen. He never made it within grabbing distance before he paused and dropped something heavy on the countertop. Dark leather and ivory parchment. A book. 

“It’s for your memories,” Mydei explained before Phainon could ask. He nudged it across the table. A glance was enough to know it was expensive but Mydei merely said, “If you run out of space, we’ll get another one.”

Judging by the thickness of leather-bound pages, that was less a possibility and more an inevitability. He could build a city from the ink and parchment. 

A number of questions flitted through his mind but he settled for the most basic. “Why?”

“You claim you’ve worked through your memories but I doubt it was a complete process.” Mydei left space for him to deny but Phainon’s lips twisted in silence, the pain and elation and resignation of being known just as snarled inside him. “Besides, leaving it untouched in the past won’t bring you closure.”

He picked up the empty book waiting to be filled. The Worldbearer never forgets. There were happier things to engrave, to preserve, like the joyful tomorrow that had become their every day. 

Had he processed each memory of each cycle? Perhaps enough to continue striving forwards without collapsing under their collective weight but nothing more. It was likely he would never manage to touch upon every excavated artefact. To carefully brush away the debris and examine the damage and details. To place it behind a glass case where it sat pristine for him to glance at every so often as a mere novelty. 

Phainon peered through his lashes. “Will you read it?”

The surprise raised Mydei’s brows but he wasn’t displeased. He nodded, resolute. “If you’d let me.”

It was a near impossible task to glance back at the long, arduous journey and roll the boulder back down the hills turned valleys without letting it run away from him entirely. But that didn’t mean he shouldn’t try. Perhaps, somewhere along his journey, he would rediscover how to dream of something other than his past self or nothing at all. Until then, and even long after, they could continue to share their dreams together.

End Notes

Me, gently holding Phainon in my palms: I love Phainon so very very much

Me, shoving Phainon into the torture machine: Time for daycare! Have fun!

When I first thought of this fic it was supposed to be more Mydei-centric… but Phainon has so many issues. So many. They never end.
